title: Mirror Formula
notes: A spherical reflecting surface acts as a spherical mirror. For paraxial rays, a concave mirror converges parallel rays to a real focus; a convex mirror makes them diverge from a virtual focus.
The centre of curvature C is distance R from pole P; paraxial focus F is halfway between, so f=R/2. Wide-angle marginal rays do not meet this approximation exactly.
Using Cartesian distances positive to the right, a concave mirror has f=−15 cm. For u=−30 cm, 1/v=1/f−1/u=−1/15+1/30=−1/30, so v=−30 cm and m=−v/u=−1.

Construct an image with a ray parallel to the principal axis (reflected through F for a concave mirror) and a ray through C (retraces itself). Their intersection locates a real image; backward extensions locate a virtual image.
Spherical aberration occurs when marginal rays focus differently from paraxial rays. A smaller aperture reduces it by excluding marginal rays.

When an object is closer to a concave mirror than the focus, the formula gives a positive v. In the Cartesian convention that positive image distance is behind the mirror, and the image is virtual, upright and enlarged. The same formula covers both the real and the virtual cases. The sign does the work.

exercises.question: A concave mirror has f = −10 cm. An object is at u = −6.0 cm. Find v and say what kind of image it is.
steps: Positive v means a virtual image behind the mirror.
m = −v/u = −(15)/(−6) = +2.5, so the image is upright and enlarged.
exercises.answer: v = +15 cm, a virtual upright image, 2.5 times as tall.
